alt: Two columns. Crime and deviance has four parts, 3.5.1 to 3.5.4, with Merton, Becker, Heidensohn, Albert Cohen, Carlen and the dark figure. Social stratification has six parts, 3.6.1 to 3.6.6, with Davis and Moore, Marx, Weber, Devine, Townsend, Murray and Walby.
caption: Paper 2 has ten content areas and twelve named sociologists.

alt: A revision grid with the four perspectives down the side (functionalism, Marxism, feminism, interactionism) and five issues across the top (crime, social control, class, poverty, power). Interactionism applies to the crime section only. Two sample cells are filled: Davis and Moore for the functionalist view of class, and Marx on ownership for the Marxist view.
caption: Perspectives down the side, issues across the top: one grid for the whole paper.

alt: Left: a small circle for crime, which breaks the law, sits inside a larger circle for deviance, which breaks social norms and need not be illegal. Right: a bar for all crime, where official statistics show only the lower part and the dark figure of unreported or unrecorded crime sits above it.
caption: Deviance is wider than crime, and official statistics miss the dark figure.

alt: Left: Marx’s account of stratification rests on one pillar, class based on ownership of the means of production. Right: Weber’s rests on three pillars, class, status and party.
caption: Marx centres on ownership; Weber adds status and party.

alt: Two sides. Davis and Moore say greater rewards for important roles make the most able compete for them, so inequality is a fair outcome of meritocratic competition. Marxists say the bourgeoisie use ownership of the means of production to exploit the proletariat, so the competition was never fair.
caption: The real disagreement is whether the competition for rewards is fair.
